topics.topic: Whether function code may access and observe /proc
questions: Is /proc present and stat-readable by function code, or must filesystem access outside the runtime and exchange directory be refused?
Must `os.scandir('/proc')` succeed and expose directory entries with zeroed timestamps, or must it be a `sandbox_violation` because it opens a path outside the exchange directory and runtime?
Is `/proc` present and observable by function code, despite the closed environment and no-filesystem rules, or must access to it fail?

quotes:
No clock through the other doors: each entry point of rule 4 added on 2026-11-03,
    and a fresh import of `time`, concludes `sandbox_violation`; a file's timestamp read
    through the stat family, on a scratch file, the code file and `/proc`, reads zero.
judgement.why: The closed environment invariant excludes `/proc`, while the required test requires function code to stat `/proc` successfully and observe a zero timestamp.

topics.topic: Exactly which stat-family timestamp fields and representations are masked, including DirEntry.stat variants and caching
questions: Exactly which fields and representations must be zero—for example `st_atime`, `st_mtime`, `st_ctime`, their `_ns` forms, the corresponding tuple positions, platform-added timestamp fields, and every result of `DirEntry.stat()` and `DirEntry.stat(follow_symlinks=False)`—and must cached results obey the same rule?
What exact observable stat-family result must the sandbox return, including the fields and representations changed and the behavior of `DirEntry.stat()` with either `follow_symlinks` value?

quotes: It MUST wrap each function named in zero_timestamps so that the stat result it gives, or the entry os.scandir yields gives, carries zero access, modification and change times in seconds and nanoseconds, whatever the file, and set sys.dont_write_bytecode to true.
judgement.why: The later runner contract specifies access, modification and change timestamps in both seconds and nanoseconds for direct stat results and entries yielded by `os.scandir`, covering the entry's stat results regardless of caching or link-following variant.

topics.topic: How permitted stat-family non-timestamp metadata and directory contents are normalized for determinism
questions: Which non-timestamp fields of stat results must be preserved, normalized, hidden or trapped so that code cannot return execution-specific filesystem identifiers?
If stat-family access to files such as `/proc` is permitted, what prevents non-timestamp metadata and directory membership from making equal inputs produce different outputs?

quotes:
A file's
   timestamps read through `os.stat`, `os.lstat`, `os.fstat`, `os.scandir` and their
   `posix` namesakes are zero, whatever the file.
The same implementation on the same input yields the same output digest twice.

It MUST wrap each function named in zero_timestamps so that the stat result it gives, or the entry os.scandir yields gives, carries zero access, modification and change times in seconds and nanoseconds, whatever the file, and set sys.dont_write_bytecode to true.
judgement.divergence: One implementer can expose a stable synthetic inode or other non-time metadata, while another can replace it with zero or hide it; function callers and agents inspecting trial outputs observe different values even though both implementations zero the specified timestamps and repeat their own result.
judgement.why: Neither State 2 nor the later runner contract specifies the observable values of non-timestamp stat metadata or directory membership, while repeatability requires an implementer to choose some stabilization or restriction.

witness.initial: An implementation with fixed inputs creates the same scratch file on each execution and returns its observed `st_ino`; the sandbox implementation must make repeated executions produce the same output digest.
events: An agent tries the implementation twice with the same trial case.
On each execution the function creates the scratch file and calls `os.stat` on it.
outcomes: One conforming sandbox returns a stable synthetic inode of `0`, so both executions output `0`.
Another conforming sandbox returns a stable synthetic inode of `1`, so both executions output `1`.
witness.observer: The agent reading the TrialExecutions sees different output values and digests between the two permitted sandbox implementations.
basis:
Every function execution, in trial and in a run alike, runs in a fresh
   isolated environment created by the sandbox: Linux `bubblewrap` with new user,
   PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces, no network interface but the namespace's own loopback — up, as bubblewrap leaves it in a new network namespace, and reaching nothing outside the execution, so K-02's "no network" holds; this is a property of how the kernel starts bubblewrap, which the kernel does not inspect or verify at run time — the start check (rule 8) asks only that a probe execution succeeds — an environment
   holding only `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` (rule 2), a read-only runtime, and one private exchange directory in which every file the code writes is
   bounded by `sandbox_scratch_bytes_max` (rule 5).

A file's
   timestamps read through `os.stat`, `os.lstat`, `os.fstat`, `os.scandir` and their
   `posix` namesakes are zero, whatever the file.
The same implementation on the same input yields the same output digest twice.

topics.topic: Which freshly imported module names must trigger a trap
questions: Which modules must cause a trap when freshly imported after removal from sys.modules: only modules named by the added list, or all modules containing any trapped entry point?
Exactly which module names cause a trap when freshly imported after removal from `sys.modules`?

judgement.why: P1 judged the same question on the same fresh-import passage and established that every module named by any supplied trap list is covered; neither that passage nor the later deciding passage has changed.

precedent.topic: Module names and name-matching rules covered by the fresh-import trap
quotes: runner_source: [BEHAVIOR] The program MUST, before it loads the code, import every module its lists name and only then replace every entry point named in raise_on_call with one that raises whatever arguments it is called with, those in raise_without_argument with ones that raise when called without an argument, every method of the class named by raise_on_every_method, and the class named by raise_unseeded when constructed without a seed or with None, and that class's seed method when called on an instance without a seed or with None (A03 rule 4: an explicitly seeded instance draws no entropy and stays usable); and install an audit hook that raises on socket, subprocess and ctypes use, on opening any path outside the exchange directory and the readable_paths, and on a fresh import of any module those lists name.
precedent.why: The later note makes the covered set every module named by any of the supplied trap lists, rather than only the newly appended State 2 paths.
